title: Certified Growth Bound for the k-th Prime ≡ 3 (mod 4)
description: The parent's Euclid-style proof of infinitely many primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) certifies more than infinitude: it bounds how fast such primes grow. We extract the interval bound (a prime ≡ 3 mod 4 always lies in (n, 4·(n+1)! − 1]), build the increasing enumeration p₃(0) < p₃(1) < … of these primes, and prove the explicit iterated-factorial tower bound p₃(k) ≤ B(k) with B(0)=3, B(k+1)=4·(B(k)+1)!−1. We contrast this astronomically loose certified bound with the true asymptotic p_k ∼ 2k·ln k from the PNT for arithmetic progressions. Fully machine-checked (0 sorry, 0 axiom, native_decide-free). This iteration adds the completeness half: p3 enumerates *exactly* the primes ≡3 (mod 4) (mem_range_p3_iff / p3_surjective, via minimality of nextP3), so with strict monotonicity 'p3 k = the k-th such prime' is now rigorous and the tower bound provably bounds every one of them. This iteration adds the sharper **primorial bound** p₃(k) ≤ 4·(∏_{i<k} p₃(i)) − 1, replacing the factorial by the product of the primes found so far, and packages it as an explicit doubly-exponential tower C with C(0)=3, C(1)=11, C(2)=131, C(3)=17291 satisfying p₃(k) ≤ C(k). It is strictly tighter than the factorial tower already at k=1 (7 ≤ 11 = C(1) < 95 = B(1)) and incomparably tighter for k≥2 (C(2)=131 vs B(2)=4·96!−1), while still honestly far from the truth p_k ∼ 2k·ln k. All new results are 0 sorry / 0 axiom, native_decide-free (kernel decide only).

overview.historicalContext:
Euclid's argument for the infinitude of primes adapts to the arithmetic progression 3 (mod 4): if p₁,…,p_k are known primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), then N = 4·p₁⋯p_k − 1 (or the cleaner N = 4·(n+1)! − 1) is ≡ 3 (mod 4) and hence has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) larger than all inputs. This is the parent entry dirichlets-theorem-oq-02.

Beyond mere infinitude, such a constructive argument certifies a *rate*: each step produces a new prime not much larger than a factorial of the previous one, giving an explicit — if wildly inefficient — upper bound on the k-th prime in the progression. The genuine growth is governed by the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions (de la Vallée Poussin, 1896), which gives π(x; 4, 3) ∼ x/(2 ln x) and hence p_k ∼ 2k·ln k. This entry makes the certified elementary bound precise and honestly contrasts it with the truth.
overview.problemStatement: The Euclid-style construction N = 4·(n+1)! − 1 certifies a prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) exceeding n. Question (OQ-02-OQ-03): what explicit lower bound on the k-th prime p_k ≡ 3 (mod 4) — equivalently, what upper bound on p_k — does this elementary construction certify, and how does it compare with the true asymptotic p_k ∼ 2k·ln k?
overview.text: We formalize the certified growth bound implicit in the elementary Euclid argument for primes ≡ 3 (mod 4): the k-th such prime is at most an explicit iterated-factorial tower B(k), versus the true p_k ∼ 2k·ln k.
overview.proofStrategy:
**1. Interval bound.** Re-deriving the parent's factor lemma, we package the construction as an interval statement: for every n there is a prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) with n < p ≤ 4·(n+1)! − 1. The upper bound comes from p ∣ N = 4·(n+1)! − 1, the lower from p ∤ (n+1)! (else p ∣ gcd(N, N+1) = 1).

**2. Next prime and enumeration.** nextP3 n := the least prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) above n (via Nat.find, well defined by the interval bound). Its minimality (Nat.find_min') certifies that no such prime is skipped. Iterating from 3 gives p3, the strictly increasing enumeration of all primes ≡ 3 (mod 4).

**3. Tower bound.** Define B(0)=3, B(k+1)=4·(B(k)+1)!−1. By induction, p3(k) ≤ B(k): the successor step chains nextP3_le_factorial with monotonicity of x ↦ 4·(x+1)!−1.

**4. Honesty check.** p3 1 = 7 while B 1 = 95: the certified bound is already >13× loose at k=1, and the gap explodes (B 2 = 4·96! − 1) — reflecting the chasm between the constructive tower and the true 2k·ln k.
keyInsights: The Euclid construction certifies not just infinitude but an explicit *interval*: a prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) always lies in (n, 4·(n+1)! − 1].

Nat.find packages 'the next prime ≡ 3 (mod 4)' cleanly, and its minimality lemma certifies the enumeration skips nothing — so p3 k is genuinely the k-th such prime, with no appeal to Mathlib's Nat.nth.
Iterating the one-step factorial bound yields an iterated-factorial tower B(k); monotonicity of x ↦ 4·(x+1)!−1 makes the induction a three-line calc.

The certified bound is astronomically loose (B 1 = 95 vs p3 1 = 7; B 2 = 4·96!−1): the elementary argument is honest about existence but says almost nothing about density, which needs the analytic PNT for APs.
The whole development is native_decide-free — the single numeric fact B 1 = 95 is discharged by kernel `decide`, keeping the axiom count at 0.
prerequisites: Elementary number theory (primes, modular arithmetic, factorials)
Euclid's argument for infinitude of primes

sections.title: File Overview
sections.summary: Motivating contrast between an elementary *certified* growth bound for the primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) and their true asymptotic density (Dirichlet). Sets up the certified factorial/primorial towers B and C and the honest gap between the provable lower bound and the truth.
sections.mathContext: Header docstring and imports framing OQ-02-OQ-03: proving explicit, kernel-checkable lower bounds on the k-th prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) and its counting function π(x; 4, 3), and quantifying how far these certified towers sit below the real n·log-scale growth.

sections.title: Step 1: The Euclid Interval Bound
sections.summary: Euclid-style existence: every n has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) exceeding a given bound, giving a prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) in a controlled interval and one larger than any N.
sections.mathContext: exists_prime_factor_three_mod_four, exists_prime_three_mod_four_in_interval and exists_prime_three_mod_four_gt: the classical Euclidean argument (a product +2 style witness) forces a new prime ≡ 3 (mod 4), bounding where the next one must appear.

sections.title: Step 2: The Next Prime and the Increasing Enumeration p3
sections.summary: Defines nextP3 (the immediate next prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) above n) and the strictly increasing enumeration p3 of all primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), proving it is prime-valued, ≡ 3 (mod 4), strictly monotone, and surjective onto that set.
sections.mathContext: nextP3 with nextP3_gt/_prime/_mod/_le_factorial; p3 with p3_prime, p3_mod, p3_strictMono, p3_le_self, p3_surjective and mem_range_p3_iff establishing that p3 enumerates exactly the primes ≡ 3 (mod 4).

sections.title: Step 3: The Certified Iterated-Factorial Tower Bound
sections.summary: Defines the factorial tower B and proves the certified upper bound p3 k ≤ B k, together with the linear lower bound and the two-sided bracket for p3.
sections.mathContext: def B (iterated-factorial tower), step_mono, p3_le_tower (p3 k ≤ B k), p3_ge_linear and p3_bracketed give an explicit, kernel-certified two-sided envelope for the k-th prime ≡ 3 (mod 4).

sections.title: Step 4: Worked Values and the Honest Contrast
sections.summary: Sanity checks at small k (p3_one, B_one) and tower_loose_at_one, quantifying how loose the certified factorial-tower bound is against the true value.
sections.mathContext: p3_one, B_one, tower_loose_at_one: worked base cases demonstrating the (large) gap between the certified bound B and the actual primes, motivating the tighter primorial tower next.

sections.title: Step 5: The Tighter Primorial Bound
sections.summary: Introduces the primorial tower C (via towerProd) and proves the sharper certified bound p3 k ≤ C k, with worked values and the fact that the primorial tower is tighter than the factorial tower.
sections.mathContext: p3_le_primorial; def towerProd, def C, C_eq, towerProd_eq_prod, p3_le_primorialTower; C_zero_eq/C_one_eq/C_two_eq; primorial_tighter_than_factorial and p3_bracketed_primorial sharpen Step 3's envelope using primorials instead of factorials.

sections.title: Step 6: The Primorial Tower Never Exceeds the Factorial Tower (C k ≤ B k)
sections.summary: Proves the (weak) domination C k ≤ B k of the primorial tower by the factorial tower, via the per-step factorial bound.
sections.mathContext: factorial_ge_mul_pred, towerProd_succ_le_factorial and C_le_B: each primorial step is dominated by the corresponding factorial step, so C k ≤ B k for all k.

sections.title: Steps 7–8: Strict Domination and the Closed-form Doubly-exponential Bound
sections.summary: Upgrades to strict domination C k < B k for k ≥ 1 (with the equality case), and derives an explicit non-recursive closed-form doubly-exponential bracket for the primorial tower C — showing the doubly-exponential growth is intrinsic.
sections.mathContext: factorial_gt_mul_pred, towerProd_succ_lt_factorial, C_lt_B, C_eq_B_iff (strict domination); four_mul_towerProd_le, C_le_doubly_exp, p3_le_doubly_exp, towerProd_ge, C_ge_doubly_exp and C_doubly_exp_bracket give a matching two-sided doubly-exponential closed form for C.

sections.title: Step 9: The Factorial Tower B Is Tower-exponential
sections.summary: Shows B grows tower-exponentially: 2^(...) lower bounds on successive B values, and 2^k · C k ≤ B (k+1), widening the gap between B and C.
sections.mathContext: two_pow_le_succ_factorial, B_succ_ge_two_pow and two_pow_C_le_B_succ establish exponential blow-up of B relative to C at each step.

sections.title: Step 10: The Ratio B / C Diverges
sections.summary: Proves B k ≥ (C k)² and m · C k ≤ B k for every m, so the ratio B/C diverges — the factorial tower outpaces the primorial tower without bound.
sections.mathContext: C_succ_add_one, C_succ_le_sq, C_mono, C_ge_add, quartic_le_two_pow, C_sq_le_B ((C k)² ≤ B k) and B_div_C_diverges: the certified factorial tower dominates every constant multiple of the primorial tower.

sections.title: Step 11: The Factorial Tower B Is Tetrational (2 ↑↑ k ≤ B k)
sections.summary: Introduces the tetration tower tower2 (2 ↑↑ k) and sandwiches it strictly between the doubly-exponential and factorial growth, giving a growth-class separation.
sections.mathContext: def tower2 (2 ↑↑ k), tower2_le_B (2 ↑↑ k ≤ B k), two_pow_le_tower2, doubly_exp_le_tower2, tower2_lt_doubly_exp_at_four and growth_class_separation separate tetrational B from the doubly-exponential C.

sections.title: Step 12: A Certified Lower Bound on the Counting Function π(x; 4, 3)
sections.summary: Defines the counting function primesCount3 for primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) up to x, and proves an unbounded certified lower bound driven by the doubly-exponential tower.
sections.mathContext: def primesCount3, card_le_primesCount3, primesCount3_mono, primesCount3_ge_of_doubly_exp, primesCount3_ge and primesCount3_unbounded: transfer the tower bounds to a certified, unbounded lower bound on π(x; 4, 3).

sections.title: Step 13: B Dominates Every Fixed Power of C
sections.summary: Strengthens Step 10: for every fixed exponent p, (C k)^p ≤ B k eventually, so B/(C^p) diverges and B/C → ∞ — the factorial tower beats every fixed polynomial power of the primorial tower.
sections.mathContext: two_pow_two_mul_le_tower2, C_pow_le_B_eventually ((C k)^p ≤ B k eventually), B_div_C_pow_diverges, tendsto_B_div_C_pow_atTop and tendsto_B_div_C_atTop: the domination of B over C holds against every fixed power, an atTop-divergence of the ratio.

conclusion.summary: The elementary Euclid construction for primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) certifies an explicit growth bound, not just infinitude: the k-th such prime is at most the iterated-factorial tower B(k) with B(0)=3, B(k+1)=4·(B(k)+1)!−1. This is proved fully (0 sorry, 0 axiom) via an interval form of the construction, the Nat.find-based enumeration p3, and a short induction. Worked values (p3 1 = 7 ≤ 95 = B 1) show the bound is honest but astronomically loose.
conclusion.implications: The result quantifies exactly how far the constructive lower bound sits from the analytic truth p_k ∼ 2k·ln k: the Euclid tower is iterated-factorial (roughly a tower of exponentials), the reality is essentially linear in k·ln k. This mirrors the shipped Bertrand/Dirichlet OQ-extensions that separate certified elementary bounds from PNT-level asymptotics. Sharpening the certified bound toward the truth provably requires analytic input (density of primes in the progression), which the elementary argument cannot supply.
openQuestions: Can the certified tower be lowered to a genuinely sub-factorial (e.g. exponential) bound while staying elementary, or is the tower intrinsic to Euclid-style iteration?
Formalize a lower bound on p_k (a certified upper bound on π(x; 4, 3)) from the same construction, isolating what needs the analytic PNT.
Extend the certified-tower framework to other progressions a (mod q) with elementary Euclid arguments (e.g. 5 mod 6, 1 mod 4 via different constructions).
